# About TruCount CPA PC

## Identity
TruCount CPA PC was founded in 2009 in Brookings, South Dakota, initially run solo for four to five years before establishing its Brookings office. The firm is led by Julie Underwood, CPA, CEO, alongside a team including Brandi Altstaetter and Christy VanSickle — both with 13 years at the firm and part of a team with 51 years of collective accounting experience — plus staff accountants Cindy Halbersma, Lexy Spilde, and Amber Hanson.

Julie, Brandi, and Christy (referred to internally as Kristy) all grew up on farms, giving the team firsthand fluency in agricultural operations rather than secondhand textbook knowledge. The firm describes its culture as welcoming, supportive, knowledgeable, and family oriented, with staff deeply personally invested in clients' lives and families — often knowing them well enough that formal quarterly meetings become unnecessary.

Mission: To give farmers, agribusiness operators, and service businesses peace of mind from knowing their numbers so they can focus on operations, make confident decisions, and never be caught off guard.

Vision: To be the trusted financial partner for farmers, agribusiness operators, and service businesses across the Midwest, acting as an extension of their team.

The firm is affiliated with AICPA, the South Dakota Society of CPAs, and the Brookings Area Chamber of Commerce. Its office is located at 2301 Research Park Way, Suite #208, Brookings, SD 57006, serving Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties in South Dakota, western Minnesota, and Logan and Shelby counties in Ohio.

## Positioning & Differentiation
TruCount's tagline is "Get out of the books and back to your business." Its positioning statement describes the firm as "full-service agriculture and professional services specialists who build deep relationships with their clients" — a blend of industry specialization and relationship-driven service.

Key differentiators include bundled services for a fixed monthly fee to avoid billing surprises, a secure online platform for real-time collaboration and data access, personalized year-round tax and business advice, and CFO-level business management insight at a fraction of the typical cost. Pricing typically follows three service package tiers, though the firm usually assesses client needs directly and provides a custom quote rather than presenting all three options upfront.

Clients most often find TruCount through referrals and online search. Their core need is consistent: wanting to know their numbers sooner rather than later so there are no surprises, and preferring full-service accounting relationships over one-off tax filing engagements.

Competitors in the Brookings market range from local full-service firms (Kinner & Company, Brian J. Hildebrant CPA, VRS CPA), a multi-location regional firm (ELO CPAs & Advisors), and national tax prep brands (H&R Block, Jackson Hewitt) to smaller local tax preparers (Hernandez Tax Service, Tax Consultants Inc.). TruCount differentiates through deep agricultural fluency, bundled monthly-fee packages, and a relationship-first approach rather than competing purely on service breadth or national brand recognition.

## Industries Served

### Farmers
TruCount helps farm operators cultivate a financially healthy enterprise with farm-fluent CPAs who understand ag-specific tax strategy. The core pain point: farmers can't find an accountant who understands agriculture or speaks their language. Notable tax opportunities the firm highlights for this niche include the R&D credit and the excess fertility deduction.

### Agribusiness Operators
TruCount provides full-service accounting and advisory for agribusiness operators managing complex multi-entity structures — such as combined farm and service-company setups. As with farmers, the primary pain point is difficulty finding an accountant who genuinely understands agriculture. The firm identifies opportunities in tax strategy content for multi-entity agribusiness structures and succession/exit planning for owners.

### Professional Services
TruCount takes the hassle out of complex accounting for professional service business owners who want a trusted financial partner, with a focus on sub-niches including chiropractors, architects, and consultants. The shared pain point across this niche: business owners are too busy running their practice to deal with bookkeeping, payroll, and tax, so accounting falls behind or gets ignored. A key tax strategy emphasized across these sub-niches is bonus depreciation — for example, guiding a chiropractor through the tax treatment of a handicapped table purchase, with potential R&D credit applicability as well.

This firm has worked alongside farm families since 2009, and the team knows a crop year doesn't run on a standard accounting calendar.

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->
## Accounting built around crop and livestock operations

A generic small-business bookkeeper treats every client the same way. Farm accounting doesn't work like that, because input costs, commodity timing, and herd economics don't behave like a retail shop's revenue.

### Crop Operations
icon: ChartLine

Input costs for seed, fertilizer, and chemicals shift throughout the season, and commodity prices move daily. TruCount tracks cost per acre and times income recognition around grain sales and hedging activity, not a generic monthly close.

### Livestock Operations
icon: ClipboardCheck

Herd tracking, feed costs, and breeding cycles raise accounting questions a standard bookkeeper rarely sees. The team separates cow-calf and feeder cattle economics so you know which side of the operation is actually making money.

### Land and Equipment Depreciation
icon: Building2

Section 179 elections, bonus depreciation, and trade-in timing on tractors and combines affect your tax bill for years, not just one season. Depreciation schedules get modeled against your real cash flow, not just whatever saves the most this April.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: bundled-farm-accounting-services.jpg | alt: "Accountant and farm client reviewing a monthly service checklist together" | query: "advisor client meeting checklist paperwork" -->
## One bundled fee covers your bookkeeping, payroll and tax planning

Most accounting firms bill by the hour or hand you a stack of one-off returns and call it done. TruCount bundles bookkeeping, payroll, and year-round tax planning into one fixed monthly fee, so you know what you're paying before the year even starts. No surprise invoice after harvest. No separate bill every time you call with a question.

Your bundle includes:
- Bookkeeping and account reconciliation, updated on a schedule that matches your operation

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->
## Tax strategies designed for multi-entity farm operations

### Entity Structuring for Multi-Entity Farms
icon: Building2

Many farm operations run a crop LLC, a cattle operation, and a separate equipment or land entity, each with different tax treatment. Entities get structured and coordinated so income, expenses, and liability sit where they should, not where they happened to land. See [entity type analysis](/services/entity-type-analysis) for how this works.

### R&D Tax Credit for Farmers
icon: Lightbulb

Testing new seed varieties, adjusting fertility programs, or developing irrigation techniques can qualify as research and development under federal tax code. Eligible activities get identified and documented so farms claim a credit most tax preparers never mention.

### Excess Fertility Deduction
icon: Sparkles

When you purchase farmland with fertility levels above the norm for the area, that excess fertility can often be deducted rather than capitalized. The calculation and documentation get built to hold up under IRS review.

### Multi-Entity Tax Planning
icon: Scale

Coordinating income and deductions across multiple entities takes planning before year-end, not after it. Read more about the firm's approach to [multi-entity farm tax strategy](/industries/agriculture/multi-entity-farm-tax-strategy).

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: multigenerational-farm-family-discussion.jpg | alt: "Two generations of a farm family reviewing documents together outdoors" | query: "farm family generations discussion outdoors" -->
## Planning for the next generation of your farm

Farms built over two or three generations don't transition smoothly by accident. If you're bringing a son, daughter, or next-generation partner into the operation, or you're the one stepping into land your parents worked, the entity structure and tax decisions made now determine how much of the farm actually survives the transfer.

TruCount helps family operations set up entities, buy-sell agreements, and gifting or transfer strategies that keep the operation intact and the tax bill manageable. This isn't a document signed once and filed away. The plan gets revisited as land values, family involvement, and tax law change, so it still fits your operation in ten years. If succession is somewhere on your horizon, [farm succession planning](/industries/agriculture/farm-succession-planning) is built specifically for operations like yours.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: farmer-checking-financials-mobile-device.jpg | alt: "Farmer checking financial data on a tablet inside a barn" | query: "farmer tablet mobile device barn" -->

Ask a question, upload a document, or check cash flow before an equipment purchase, all without waiting on a scheduled call. ## The everyday accounting challenges service business owners face

Service businesses run on billable hours, project fees, and retainers, which makes cash flow look different every month. Owners we talk to in Brookings mention the same handful of issues, and by the time tax season arrives, last year's numbers can feel like ancient history.

- Inconsistent monthly revenue from project-based billing or retainer clients
- Payroll complexity once a team grows past one or two employees
- Estimated tax payments calculated on guesswork instead of current numbers
- Wanting to know where the business stands mid-year, not just at filing time
- No single place to see cash flow, payroll, and tax data together

## Guidance for growing and multi-entity service companies

Service businesses that add partners, open a second location, or spin off a related company need more than clean books. They need someone thinking about structure and long-term strategy alongside the day-to-day numbers, which is where CFO-level insight matters most.

### Entity Type Analysis
icon: Scale

Sole proprietor, S-corp, partnership, multi-entity structure: the right answer changes as your service business grows, and getting it wrong costs real money in taxes and liability exposure. [Review entity type analysis](/services/entity-type-analysis).

### Accounting System Setup
icon: Cog

A system built for a five-person shop won't hold up at twenty employees. We set up and optimize accounting systems so your reporting scales with the business instead of falling behind it. [See accounting system setup](/services/accounting-system-setup).

### Retirement Plan Analysis
icon: PiggyBank

Offering a retirement plan helps recruit and retain talent, but overpaying for the wrong plan hurts margins. We help service businesses choose a plan that fits the team and the budget. [Learn about retirement plan analysis](/services/retirement-plan-analysis).

### Bookkeeping

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Bookkeeping built for Brookings farmers and business owners

You didn't start your operation to spend evenings matching receipts to bank statements. Between planting windows, herd schedules, or a full client calendar, bookkeeping is the task that gets pushed to "later" until later becomes a scramble every March. TruCount CPA PC handles the day-to-day recordkeeping for farmers, agribusiness operators, and service businesses across Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties, so the numbers are accurate and current without you touching a spreadsheet.

This isn't a one-off data-entry service. Bookkeeping at TruCount feeds directly into tax planning and business decisions throughout the year, for one fixed monthly fee. No shoebox of receipts, no billing surprises, no guessing where your business stands. Just clean books and time back for the work only you can do.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: bookkeeper-reviewing-transactions.jpg | alt: "Bookkeeper classifying transactions and reconciling accounts on a laptop" | query: "bookkeeper working laptop office" -->
## What our bookkeeping service covers

Good bookkeeping is more than data entry. It's the foundation that makes tax season painless and business decisions confident. Here's what's included every month:

- Transaction classification, so every deposit and expense lands in the right account
- Expense tracking tied to categories that matter at tax time, not generic buckets
- Monthly account reconciliation across your bank, credit card, and loan accounts
- Clean, accurate financial statements you can hand to a lender or read yourself
- Ongoing coordination with our [tax planning](/services/tax) and [outsourced accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) teams, so your books and your strategy never disconnect

We don't hand you a spreadsheet in December and call it done. Your books stay current month to month, which means when tax season or a loan application shows up, the numbers are already there.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: farm-equipment-financial-records.jpg | alt: "Farmer reviewing equipment purchase records alongside financial statements" | query: "farmer reviewing paperwork tractor" -->
## Bookkeeping designed around agriculture and agribusiness cycles

Generic bookkeeping software doesn't know the difference between a fertilizer prepay and a routine operating expense, or that a grain sale in January might belong to last year's crop. Farm income doesn't arrive on a tidy monthly schedule, and neither do the input costs, equipment purchases, or land payments that come with it.

We've worked with farmers and agribusiness operators across South Dakota, western Minnesota, and Logan and Shelby counties in Ohio long enough to build our processes around how ag actually operates: seasonal income timing, equipment depreciation schedules, and multi-entity structures where a farm operation and a separate equipment or trucking entity need to stay untangled on paper even as they work together in the field. If your operation spans multiple entities, our [multi-entity farm tax strategy](/industries/agriculture/multi-entity-farm-tax-strategy) work builds directly on the books we keep for you.

A local bookkeeper who's never worked a 1245 property sale or an excess fertility deduction will miss things. We won't.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: online-platform-remote-access.jpg | alt: "Business owner viewing financial dashboard on a laptop from a workshop" | query: "business owner laptop dashboard remote" -->
## Real-time access through a secure online platform

Bookkeeping used to mean waiting for a phone call or driving across town to drop off a folder. Our secure online platform gives you real-time access to your financial data from wherever you are, whether that's the shop, the combine cab, or a job site three counties over.

You can see current balances, upload documents, and message our team without waiting for office hours. It's collaboration that happens on your schedule, not ours, and it means no more digging through a shoebox of receipts or reconciling a spreadsheet you haven't opened since last quarter. Everything lives in one place, updated continuously, visible to you and to us at the same time.

That kind of access is standard at national firms with big technology budgets. We built it into a fixed monthly fee for a Brookings-based agribusiness or service business, not just a large corporate client.

### Payroll
URL: /services/payroll

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Payroll that runs itself so you don't have to

Payroll shouldn't be the reason you're still at your desk on a Friday night. Between tracking hours, calculating withholdings, filing tax deposits, and keeping up with rules that change every year, payroll eats time that should go toward running your operation. At TruCount CPA, payroll isn't something we bolt on as an afterthought or bill by the hour. It's built into our [outsourced accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) relationships alongside bookkeeping and tax planning, so you get one fixed monthly fee and one team that already knows your business. Julie Underwood, CPA, and the TruCount team handle the deadlines and the paperwork. You get back to the barn, the job site, or the client meeting that actually needs your attention. That's the idea behind our tagline: get out of the books and back to your business.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: farm-payroll-review.jpg | alt: "Farmer and accountant reviewing payroll records together outdoors" | query: "farmer reviewing paperwork accountant" -->
## Payroll built for farm and agribusiness pay cycles

Farm payroll isn't office payroll. You've got seasonal crews during planting and harvest, family members drawing wages alongside hired hands, and pay schedules that shift with the weather instead of the calendar. Add in operations that stretch across South Dakota, western Minnesota, and Logan and Shelby Counties in Ohio, and the withholding rules multiply fast.

TruCount CPA has run payroll for [agribusiness operators](/industries/agriculture) across Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties for well over a decade. We know how to classify family labor correctly, handle multi-state withholding for operations that cross state lines, and keep seasonal hires compliant without slowing down your crew. Payroll runs on our secure online platform, so you can check hours, pay stubs, and deposits from the tractor cab or the shop office. No guessing whether a check cleared or a filing went out on time.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: office-payroll-meeting.jpg | alt: "Service business owner reviewing payroll reports with an accountant at a desk" | query: "office meeting reviewing documents" -->
## Payroll support for professional service teams

Service businesses run on people: salaried staff, hourly contractors, and a benefits package that has to withhold correctly every pay period. Miss a deduction or misclassify a contractor, and you're looking at penalties instead of growth.

TruCount CPA manages pay runs, benefits withholding, and contractor payments for [professional service firms](/industries/service-based-businesses) across Brookings and the surrounding counties. Your team gets paid accurately and on time, without you double-checking the math every pay period. Because payroll runs through the same platform as your bookkeeping and tax planning, nothing falls through the cracks between systems. You stay focused on billable work and client relationships, and TruCount stays focused on the filings, deposits, and compliance details that keep the IRS and the state off your back.

You'll never wonder what's included or what costs extra, because payroll is part of your bundled outsourced accounting service from day one.

## Tax preparation that gets you back to your business

Tax season shouldn't take over your calendar for three months and then disappear until next April. At TruCount CPA PC, tax preparation and planning run all year, not just in the weeks before a deadline. Farmers watching commodity prices, agribusiness operators managing input costs, and service-based business owners in Brookings all need a plan that adjusts as their numbers change, not a form filled out after the fact.

That's the idea behind our tagline: get out of the books and back to your business. Julie Underwood, CPA, and the team built TruCount CPA PC in 2009 to give South Dakota business owners a way to know their tax position before December 31, not after. When you know your numbers sooner, decisions get easier and surprises get rarer.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: year-round-tax-planning.jpg | alt: "Business owner and CPA reviewing tax planning documents on a laptop" | query: "business owner accountant laptop meeting" -->
## Year-round tax planning instead of once-a-year filing

Most tax preparation happens backward: a business owner hands over a shoebox of receipts in March and finds out in April what they owe. That model leaves no room to change anything. TruCount CPA PC works the other direction. Tax planning happens throughout the year on a fixed monthly fee, bundled with the rest of your accounting work, so there's no bill that shows up out of nowhere in tax season.

Everything runs through a secure online platform, so you can see where your business stands in real time instead of waiting for a year-end phone call. Quarterly check-ins flag tax moves while there's still time to act on them, whether that's adjusting estimated payments, timing equipment purchases, or restructuring how income flows through your entities. By the time your return is due, there's nothing left to figure out. It's already been planned for, reviewed, and confirmed with you along the way.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: farm-tax-strategy-review.jpg | alt: "Farmer and accountant discussing tax documents in a farm office" | query: "farmer accountant discussing paperwork" -->
## Specialized tax strategy for farmers and agribusiness

Farm tax returns carry rules that a general practice CPA might see once a year. TruCount CPA PC works with farmers and agribusiness operators across Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties every season, which means these strategies get applied before December, not discovered after the return is filed.

- R&D credit review for qualifying farm activities, including seed trials, precision ag testing, and new equipment integration
- Excess fertility deduction analysis for purchased farmland with above-average soil nutrient levels
- Multi-entity structuring for operations that combine a farm with a trucking company, feed lot, or other related business
- Depreciation timing and Section 179 planning tied to equipment purchases
- Income averaging and self-employment tax planning for years with swings in farm income

These strategies save real money without inviting audit risk, because they're grounded in current IRS guidance for agricultural taxpayers, and they get revisited every year as your operation changes.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: service-business-tax-planning.jpg | alt: "Small business owner discussing tax strategy with an accountant" | query: "small business owner accountant discussion" -->
## Tax support built for service-based businesses

Consultants, contractors, medical practices, and other service-based businesses in Brookings face a different set of questions than a farm operation does. The biggest one is usually entity structure: is an S-corp saving money, or is it just adding payroll complexity without a real tax benefit? TruCount CPA PC runs the numbers on reasonable salary, distributions, and self-employment tax before recommending a structure, not after you've already filed as one.

Retirement plans get the same treatment. A SEP IRA, SIMPLE IRA, or 401(k) each carries different tax timing and contribution limits, and the right choice depends on payroll size and cash flow, not a generic recommendation. We walk through the tradeoffs in plain terms, connect the retirement decision to your entity structure, and revisit both whenever your business grows enough to change the math.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: bundled-services-checklist.jpg | alt: "Desk with financial statements, calculator, and payroll documents organized for review" | query: "financial documents desk organized" -->
## What your outsourced accounting department includes

One fixed monthly fee covers the full scope of your back office, not a menu you have to reassemble every year. Here's what's included:

- Bookkeeping: daily transaction classification, expense tracking, and account reconciliation so your books are current, not caught up in April.
- Payroll coordination: wage calculations, tax filings, and direct deposit handled so paydays never slip.
- Tax planning and preparation: year-round strategy sessions plus your return, coordinated by the same team that manages your monthly books.
- Advisory and CFO-level insight: margin analysis, cash flow forecasting, and entity guidance delivered in plain language, not jargon.
- Secure digital access: real-time financial data and direct messaging with your TruCount team through our online platform.

Compare that to a one-off tax return or an hourly bookkeeper billing you every time you call with a question. Bundled, fixed-fee outsourced accounting means the advice is already paid for, so you ask the question instead of avoiding the invoice.

## Built for farmers and agribusiness operators

Generic outsourced accounting firms treat a farm like any small business. It isn't. Grain prices swing, equipment purchases hit in the fourth quarter, and cash flow depends on a harvest that may or may not cooperate with your loan payment schedule.

TruCount works with farmers and agribusiness operators across Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties, plus operations in western Minnesota and Logan and Shelby counties in Ohio. We structure multi-entity farm and service business setups so income, equipment, and land are tracked where they actually belong, not lumped together and guessed at come tax time.

We also flag opportunities generalist firms miss: the R&D credit for on-farm process improvements, and the excess fertility deduction when soil test data supports it. Both require documentation most bookkeepers never ask for, and both can put real dollars back into your operation.

Seasonal cash flow gets planned for, not reacted to. You'll know in March what your tax bill looks like in September, and you'll know it because someone ran the numbers, not because you guessed.

## Personal tax help that goes beyond a once-a-year form

If your personal return is really a snapshot of your farm, your LLC, or your consulting business, a once-a-year drop-off with a seasonal preparer was never going to cut it. National chains and pop-up tax offices close their doors in April and reopen in January, leaving you to guess at your own numbers the other nine months. TruCount CPA PC works differently. Julie Underwood, CPA, and the team have spent 13 years in Brookings building relationships with farmers, agribusiness operators, and service business owners whose personal taxes are tied directly to how their operations perform. That familiarity is what catches deductions, flags problems early, and keeps April from ever feeling like a surprise.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: farm-family-tax-review.jpg | alt: "Farm couple reviewing personal tax documents with their CPA" | query: "farm family meeting accountant paperwork" -->
## Built for farm families and business owners with complex returns

A personal return for someone running a grain operation, a service business, or a multi-entity farm structure looks nothing like a standard 1040. There's farm income and expense reporting, self-employment tax calculations, K-1s from partnerships, and depreciation schedules that all have to line up with what's happening on the business side. Miss the connection between the two, and you either overpay or invite a notice.

This is where niche experience pays off. TruCount works with farmers and agribusiness operators across Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties, plus clients in western Minnesota and Logan and Shelby counties in Ohio, and that concentration means we know where the money hides. We look for opportunities like the R&D credit for qualifying farm activities and the excess fertility deduction on purchased farmland, credits and deductions that general preparers routinely overlook because they don't see enough ag returns to recognize them.

No mailing paper. No sitting in a waiting room.

- Upload documents securely from anywhere, any time of day

### Entity type analysis
URL: /services/entity-type-analysis

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Choosing the right structure shapes your tax bill and your risk

Deciding whether to run your operation as a sole proprietorship, LLC, S corporation, partnership, or a multi-entity setup isn't a paperwork formality. It's the decision that determines how much of your income lands in your pocket instead of going to self-employment tax, how exposed your personal assets are if something goes sideways, and how cleanly the business transfers to the next generation or a buyer.

Farm and service business owners across Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties often inherit a structure someone set up years ago, with little explanation of the tradeoffs. Growth changes the math. A structure that made sense at $80,000 in revenue can cost real money at $400,000.

Entity type analysis at TruCount CPA PC means sitting down with your actual numbers, your family situation, and your growth plans, then recommending a structure with a clear reason attached, not a guess.

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: horizontal -->
## How we evaluate your business structure

Entity analysis isn't a one-time form you fill out and forget. Julie Underwood, CPA, and the TruCount team walk through your business the same way each time, so the recommendation holds up.

### Review your current setup
We start with how your business is structured today, what elections are in place, and whether they still fit your income level and goals.

### Model your income and growth
We look at where your revenue is heading over the next two to three years, since a structure that saves money now can cost you at higher income levels.

### Weigh family and ownership dynamics
Multi-generational farms and multi-owner service firms need structures that account for who's involved, who's exiting, and who's taking over.

### Handle the filings, start to finish
Once we recommend a structure, we prepare and file the related state and federal paperwork, including South Dakota entity filings, so nothing falls on your desk.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: farm-entity-structure-review.jpg | alt: "Farm business owner and CPA reviewing entity structure paperwork at a table" | query: "farmer meeting with accountant office" -->
## Entity strategy built for farms and agribusiness

Farm operations rarely fit into one entity. A lot of the farm families we work with in the Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody county area run land in one entity, machinery and operations in another, and sometimes a separate custom-work or trucking business layered on top. Structured correctly, that separation protects the land from operating liability and sets up cleaner succession when the next generation steps in.

Entity structure also affects which deductions and credits are even available to you. The R&D credit isn't just for tech companies. Farmers testing new seed varieties, feed rations, or irrigation methods can qualify, but only if the entity claiming it is set up right. The same goes for the excess fertility deduction on purchased farmland. We factor both into how we structure and time your entity elections, and we coordinate the analysis with our [multi-entity farm tax strategy](/industries/agriculture/multi-entity-farm-tax-strategy) work and [farm succession planning](/industries/agriculture/farm-succession-planning) so the structure you build today still works when ownership changes hands.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: service-business-owner-consultation.jpg | alt: "Service business owner discussing entity options with an accountant" | query: "professional consulting small business owner office" -->
## Entity guidance for service-based business owners

Agriculture isn't the only place entity choice matters. Consultants, contractors, and professional service firms across Brookings face a different but equally consequential set of questions: at what income level does S-corp status start saving on self-employment tax, how does payroll need to be structured once you make that election, and what happens to your entity when you sell or hand the business off.

We've worked through these questions with [service-based business](/industries/service-based-businesses) owners who were paying self-employment tax on income that could have been split between reasonable salary and distributions. Getting the structure right also sets up a cleaner path when you're ready to think about an [exit or sale](/industries/service-based-businesses/exit-planning), since buyers and lenders care about how a business is organized, not just what it earns.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: sole-proprietor-llc-conversion.jpg | alt: "Business owner signing entity conversion documents with accountant" | query: "small business owner signing documents" -->
## Converting from a sole proprietorship or restructuring an existing entity

Most of the owners who come to us for entity work aren't starting from scratch. They're outgrowing a sole proprietorship, or they inherited an LLC or S-corp election from a previous accountant that no longer fits their income or goals. Restructuring is a real transition, and we handle it as part of an ongoing relationship, not a one-time project you're left to manage alone.

Here's what's typically involved:

- Comparing your current tax position against alternative structures using your actual financials
- Filing the entity formation or election paperwork with the state and IRS
- Setting up or adjusting payroll if you're moving to S-corp status
- Updating your [accounting system](/services/accounting-system-setup) and books to reflect the new structure
- Coordinating the change with your existing [bookkeeping and tax](/services/tax) work so nothing gets missed at year-end

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->

### Accounting system setup
URL: /services/accounting-system-setup

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Get an accounting system built around how your business runs

If your books live in three different spreadsheets, or your QuickBooks file was set up by someone who left the company two years ago, you already know the cost. Missed transactions. Numbers that don't match the bank. Hours spent hunting for information that should take seconds to find. TruCount CPA PC has been solving this for Brookings, SD area farms, agribusinesses, and service companies since 2009. We don't hand you a generic template and wish you luck. We build a chart of accounts, software setup, and reporting structure around your actual operation, whether that's a grain and livestock farm in Kingsbury County or a professional services firm managing multiple client contracts. The goal is simple: a system you can trust the moment you open it.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: accounting-software-setup-desk.jpg | alt: "Accountant configuring accounting software on a laptop at a desk" | query: "accountant setting up software laptop" -->
## What our accounting system setup includes

A good setup isn't just picking software off a shelf. It's making sure every piece talks to the others, so your numbers are accurate the first time and every time after.

- Software selection matched to your business size, industry, and how you actually operate day to day
- Chart of accounts customization built around your revenue streams, cost centers, and entity structure
- Bank feed and payroll integration so transactions flow in automatically instead of getting keyed by hand
- Setup on TruCount's secure online platform, giving you real-time access and letting our team collaborate with you without waiting on emailed spreadsheets
- Reporting structure designed to answer the questions you actually ask, not generic templates nobody reads

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: farm-fields-accounting-records.jpg | alt: "Farmer reviewing financial records with crop fields visible outside" | query: "farmer reviewing paperwork office" -->
## Built for farm and agribusiness accounting realities

Farm accounting doesn't fit neatly into off-the-shelf software defaults. You need enterprise-level tracking that separates crop income from livestock income, equipment depreciation schedules that hold up at tax time, and cash flow reporting that accounts for the fact that most of your revenue lands in a six-week window each fall. Generic bookkeeping setups miss all of it. TruCount's ag clients across Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties get a system built to track these realities from day one, along with year-round guidance on opportunities like the R&D credit for qualifying farm activities and the excess fertility deduction, both of which require the underlying accounting to be structured correctly to claim. If your current setup can't answer "which enterprise made money this year" in under a minute, it's not built for your operation.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: service-business-owner-laptop-review.jpg | alt: "Service business owner reviewing financial reports on a laptop screen" | query: "small business owner reviewing laptop reports" -->
## A system that fits service-based businesses too

Agriculture isn't the only client we build for. Professional services firms come to us with a different set of tangles: job costing that doesn't tie back to actual profitability, recurring billing that's tracked in someone's memory instead of the system, or multiple entities whose numbers need to stay separate but visible in one place. We set up your chart of accounts to track profitability by project, client, or service line, connect recurring billing so invoices go out on schedule, and structure multi-entity reporting so ownership sees the full picture without wading through five different logins. Whether you run a single-location practice or a small group of related companies, the system should make decisions easier, not harder.

### Retirement plan analysis
URL: /services/retirement-plan-analysis

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Find the right retirement plan without overpaying for it

A SEP IRA sounds simple until you're the one filling out the paperwork every March, wondering if it's still the right fit now that your operation has grown. Retirement plan analysis at TruCount CPA PC starts with a plain question: what are you actually trying to accomplish, and which plan gets you there without extra cost or complexity?

We work with farmers, agribusiness operators, and service business owners across Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties to match retirement plan structure to real numbers, not a generic recommendation pulled from a brochure. SEP IRAs, solo 401(k)s, SIMPLE IRAs, and traditional 401(k) plans each carry different contribution limits, administrative costs, and employee requirements. Picking the wrong one means overpaying for features you don't need, or missing contribution room you do.

This is guidance grounded in your tax return and your goals, not a stack of forms to sign.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: farmer-retirement-planning-review.jpg | alt: "Farmer reviewing retirement account paperwork at kitchen table" | query: "farmer reviewing financial documents home" -->
## Retirement planning built around the realities of farm income

Farm income doesn't arrive on a predictable schedule. Grain sales, livestock markets, and crop insurance payouts can swing a year's cash position by six figures, which makes standard retirement advice built for salaried employees mostly useless for production agriculture.

A retirement plan analysis for a farm operation has to account for variable income timing, land and equipment purchases competing for the same dollars, and succession plans that may hand the operation to the next generation before a traditional retirement age. A SEP IRA might let you contribute heavily in a strong year and scale back in a lean one. A solo 401(k) might open higher contribution limits if you're running the farm without employees. The right answer depends on your entity structure, your equipment plan, and whether you're already working with us on [farm succession planning](/industries/agriculture/farm-succession-planning).

We look at your full financial picture before recommending a plan, not just your birth date and income bracket.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: multi-entity-farm-family-meeting.jpg | alt: "Farm family and advisor discussing retirement plans for multiple business entities" | query: "family business meeting farm operation" -->
## Retirement options for agribusiness and multi-entity operations

Plenty of farm families also run a trucking company, an ag retail operation, or a custom application business alongside the row crop operation. Each entity has its own payroll and its own owners, and possibly its own retirement plan rules, which gets complicated fast when the same family draws income from all of them.

Multi-entity retirement planning starts with understanding how the businesses are structured. A SEP IRA at one entity and a solo 401(k) at another might both be technically legal and still leave contribution room on the table, or trigger controlled-group rules you didn't know applied. We review your entity setup alongside our [multi-entity farm tax strategy](/industries/agriculture/multi-entity-farm-tax-strategy) work to recommend a retirement approach that works across every business the family owns, not just the one that files first.

The goal is one coordinated plan, not a patchwork of accounts nobody's tracking.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: service-business-owner-benefits-planning.jpg | alt: "Service business owner reviewing employee retirement benefits options with advisor" | query: "small business owner meeting advisor office" -->
## Retirement plans that fit service-based business owners and their teams

Running a service business means competing for good employees, and a retirement benefit is often what decides between two job offers. It also means weighing your own retirement savings against payroll, software, and everything else pulling from the same account.

A retirement plan analysis for a professional services firm weighs owner contribution limits against what a match or profit-sharing formula costs across your whole staff. Considerations we walk through with clients:

- How much you want to contribute for yourself versus what you can realistically offer employees
- Whether a SIMPLE IRA's lower administrative burden outweighs a 401(k)'s higher contribution ceiling
- How employee turnover affects vesting schedules and ongoing plan complexity
- Whether a profit-sharing formula can reward long-tenured staff without straining cash flow

We serve professional services and other [service-based businesses](/industries/service-based-businesses) throughout the Brookings area with the same fixed-fee approach we use for every client.

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: vertical -->
## How a retirement plan analysis works with TruCount

### Review your current accounts
We start by looking at what's already in place, existing IRAs, old 401(k)s, or a plan you inherited from a prior accountant, and note what's working and what isn't.

### Assess your business structure and cash flow
We review your entity type, seasonal income patterns, and payroll to understand what contribution levels and plan types actually fit your business.

### Compare plan options side by side
We lay out SEP IRA, solo 401(k), SIMPLE IRA, and traditional 401(k) options with real contribution limits and administrative costs specific to your situation.

### Get a clear recommendation
You receive a straightforward recommendation you can act on, delivered through our secure online platform along with the reasoning behind it. No surprise invoice, since this analysis is included in our bundled monthly service.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Retirement planning as part of your year-round financial picture

Retirement plan analysis works best when it isn't a one-time project. Contribution limits, entity structure, and income all shift year to year, especially for farm and agribusiness clients, so a plan that made sense two years ago might not fit today.

Because we already handle [tax planning](/services/tax) and [bookkeeping](/services/bookkeeping) for many of our clients, we can flag when a retirement plan needs a second look, before it becomes a missed contribution deadline or a mismatched entity structure. One advisor, one set of books, one fixed monthly fee. No juggling a separate financial advisor who doesn't see your tax return or your cash flow.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: brookings-cpa-consultation-handshake.jpg | alt: "CPA and business owner shaking hands after a consultation meeting" | query: "business handshake meeting office consultation" -->
## Get a retirement plan analysis for your farm or business

If you're not sure whether your current retirement plan still fits your operation, or you're setting one up for the first time, let's look at the numbers together. We work with farmers, agribusiness operators, and service business owners across Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties, plus clients in western Minnesota and Ohio, through a secure online platform that keeps everything accessible in one place.

## Find the guidance you need in one place

Running a farm or a service business means you already have enough on your plate without decoding tax jargon at 9 p.m. This library pulls together the guides, tools, and explainers our team at TruCount CPA PC uses every day with clients across Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties, plus growing operations in western Minnesota and Logan and Shelby Counties, Ohio. <!-- block: content-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Farm and agribusiness tax planning resources

Farmers and agribusiness operators face tax rules that never show up in a general small-business guide. These resources cover the credits and structures we see save real money for row-crop, livestock, and ag-service operations across South Dakota.

### R&D credit for farmers
photo: rd-credit-farm-fields.jpg
query: farmer walking crop field research

Plenty of farm operations qualify for the federal R&D credit through seed trials, irrigation testing, or new feed formulations, and never claim it. This guide walks through what counts as qualified research activity on a working farm.
[Read more](/industries/agriculture)

### Excess fertility deduction
photo: soil-testing-farm-field.jpg
query: soil testing farm field agriculture

If you bought land with above-average soil fertility already built in, part of that purchase price may be deductible as excess fertility rather than depreciated over decades. We explain how the deduction works and what documentation the IRS expects.
[Read more](/industries/agriculture)

### Multi-entity farm and service company structuring
photo: farm-business-paperwork-desk.jpg
query: farm business documents desk

Running the row-crop operation, the trucking arm, and the equipment LLC as separate entities can cut your tax bill and protect assets, but only when they're structured correctly from the start.
[Read more](/industries/agriculture/multi-entity-farm-tax-strategy)

### Multi-generational farm transition planning
photo: farm-family-generations-field.jpg
query: farm family generations outdoors

Passing the operation to the next generation without a tax bill that outlives the farm takes years of planning, not a single meeting the year someone decides to retire.
[Read more](/industries/agriculture/farm-succession-planning)

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: bookkeeper-reviewing-invoices.jpg | alt: "Bookkeeper reviewing invoices and receipts at a desk" | query: "bookkeeper reviewing invoices office" -->

- Setting up expense categories that make tax time faster, not slower
- Payroll tax deposit deadlines and the penalty triggers small employers miss
- Choosing between cash and accrual accounting as a service business grows
- Picking accounting software that fits the business instead of forcing the owner to adapt to it

See how [bookkeeping](/services/bookkeeping), [payroll](/services/payroll), and [accounting system setup](/services/accounting-system-setup) work together under a single bundled fee.

## Business entity and retirement planning insights

Choosing an entity structure or a retirement plan isn't something an owner should have to guess at, or pay a lawyer by the hour to explain twice. These resources break down the decisions that come up most for growing farms and service businesses in Brookings and across South Dakota.

Our entity type analysis resources cover the real trade-offs between an LLC, S-corp, and C-corp for a farm operation or a service business, including the state and federal filings that follow whichever structure is chosen. ## Payroll and bookkeeping resource links

South Dakota employers still need federal forms even without a state income tax to withhold. W-4s for new hires, W-9s for contractors, and the state's new-hire reporting form all connect to your [payroll](/services/payroll) setup, and TruCount pulls the right version each time regulations shift. Bookkeeping clients submit receipts, statements, and invoices through the same portal used for tax documents, so nothing gets emailed twice or lost in a spam filter. <!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: farm-agribusiness-records.jpg | alt: "Farmer reviewing agricultural tax records and soil test documents" | query: "farmer reviewing paperwork agricultural office" -->
## Agriculture and agribusiness specific resources

Farm and agribusiness clients carry document needs that a generic tax checklist skips entirely. If you're testing new seed varieties, cover crop mixes, or precision ag equipment, keep records supporting the R&D credit, including trial notes, invoices, and time logs tied to the experimentation. If you've applied lime, gypsum, or other soil amendments to bring fertility up on newly purchased ground, hold onto soil test results and the closing statement, since those support an excess fertility deduction. Our [agriculture](/industries/agriculture) practice keeps a running list of what qualifies and what documentation the IRS actually wants to see, so you're not reconstructing records from memory two years later.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Helpful external links and state resources

Some forms don't originate with us, and there's no reason to pretend otherwise. For federal filings, the [IRS forms and publications page](https://www.irs.gov/forms-instructions) is the source we point clients to directly. South Dakota entity paperwork, including Articles of Organization and annual reports, runs through the [SD Secretary of State's business portal](https://sosenterprise.sd.gov). Sales tax and use tax questions route to the [SD Department of Revenue](https://dor.sd.gov). If you're weighing a SEP-IRA against a Simple IRA or a 401(k) for your team, our [retirement plan analysis](/services/retirement-plan-analysis) service walks through the paperwork before you commit to a plan structure that costs more than it should.

### Refund tracker
URL: /resources/refund-tracker

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Check your federal and state refund status in one place

Wondering where your refund is? You don't need to dig through bookmarks or guess which government site to trust. The IRS "Where's My Refund?" tool at irs.gov tracks federal returns, and the South Dakota Department of Revenue handles state-level questions for filers in Brookings, Kingsbury, and Moody counties. TruCount CPA PC didn't build these tools, and we won't pretend we did, but we know how to read them and explain what they're telling you.

For federal refunds, visit irs.gov/refunds and enter your details directly. South Dakota has no state income tax on individuals, so most of our clients only need the federal tool, though business filers with multi-state activity may need to check other states' portals depending on where they operate. If a status message confuses you or looks stuck, that's exactly the kind of question our team answers every day during filing season.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: refund-checklist-documents.jpg | alt: "Tax documents and calculator laid out on a desk for refund status check" | query: "tax documents desk paperwork" -->
## What to have ready before you check your refund

The IRS and state tools ask for the same basic information every time. Having it ready saves you a second trip back to the site.

- Your Social Security number or, for business entities, your EIN
- Your exact filing status (single, married filing jointly, head of household, etc.)
- The exact refund amount shown on your return, down to the dollar
- Your filing date, or an estimate if you're not sure
- Confirmation of whether you e-filed or mailed a paper return

Ag producers filing under a farm entity and service business owners filing under an LLC or S-corp should pull the EIN from the actual return, not a bank statement or prior-year document. A mismatched number is the most common reason these tools return an error instead of a status.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: farm-office-tax-review.jpg | alt: "Farm business owner reviewing tax paperwork at a kitchen table" | query: "farmer reviewing paperwork office" -->
## Typical refund timelines for farm, business, and individual returns

Most e-filed individual returns with direct deposit see a refund in 21 days or less, according to the IRS. Paper returns take longer, often 6 to 8 weeks, and that gap widens during peak season in March and April.

Farm and agribusiness returns tend to move slower simply because they're more complex. Multi-entity operations, depreciation schedules, and returns claiming credits like the R&D credit for farm operations or the excess fertility deduction often get pulled for additional review before the refund releases. That's not a red flag on your return, it's standard IRS process for anything outside a simple wage-and-standard-deduction filing. Service-based business owners filing under an S-corp or partnership structure should expect similar timelines to other business entities rather than individual return speed.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: accountant-explaining-tax-notice.jpg | alt: "Accountant pointing to a tax notice while explaining it to a client" | query: "accountant explaining document client" -->
## Why your refund may be delayed or different than expected

A refund that's smaller than expected, or later than expected, almost always has a specific cause. Credits under review, like agricultural R&D claims or excess fertility deductions, can add processing time while the IRS verifies documentation. A prior-year balance owed, even a small one, will reduce or offset this year's refund automatically.

Entity structure issues cause delays too. If a farm or service business changed its structure mid-year, from a sole proprietorship to an LLC or from a partnership to an S-corp, mismatched EINs between systems can stall processing. None of these are unusual, and none of them mean something went wrong with your return. They mean the IRS is doing exactly what it's supposed to do with a more complex filing.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: color-bg -->
## Questions about your refund? We're already tracking it with you

Here's the thing about refund tools: they tell you a status, not a reason. If your refund looks delayed or off, calling the IRS means a long hold and a script read by someone who's never seen your return. Calling us means talking to someone who prepared it.

Clients on our secure online platform can see their filed return, supporting documents, and prior communications in one place, year-round, not just during tax season. Julie Underwood, CPA, and our team at TruCount CPA PC review every return before it's filed, so when a question comes up about a refund amount or a credit under review, we already know the answer. Reach out directly instead of guessing at what a status update means.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: cpa-consultation-handshake.jpg | alt: "CPA shaking hands with a small business client after a consultation" | query: "cpa consultation handshake office" -->
## Get personalized tax support beyond refund tracking

Refund tracking is a small piece of a much bigger picture. TruCount CPA PC bundles tax preparation, bookkeeping, and year-round advisory into one fixed monthly fee, so farmers, agribusiness operators, and service business owners in Brookings and across the Midwest always know their numbers, not just their refund status. Ready for a tax relationship that works all year, not just in April? [Schedule a consultation](/contact) and let's talk about what your business actually needs.
